description:
Nutritional Value:

The nuts are edible and sweet, and were a food source for Native Americans and early settlers, who also used them to make "hickory milk". 

Uksak Ulhkomo literally translates as "hickory nuts mixed with water". In English, it is usually called "hickory milk". It was made in two different forms. One was a thick liquid, intended to be used soon after preparation, by adding it to stew, as a dip for traditional breads, or as a drizzle. The other version of Uksak Ulhkomo is a kind of hickory nut ball, which could be stored for a while before being dropped into a boiling stew. In either form, hickory milk is rich, very tasty, and filling. It contains a good balance of fats and provides complex carbohydrates, protein, and more calories than most other wild plant foods.

Kingnut and Shagbark were Choctaw favorites for Uksak Ulhkomo,

description:
1. While walking along my property 1 individual of the Shagbark Hickory (Carya ovata) was seen on the property.
2. The weather was partly cloudy early in the morning then became sunny in the afternoon. The high for the day was 81 degrees with a low of 60 degrees. It was 80 degrees when the tree was found.
3. Other species seen included Bigtooth Aspen (Populus grandidentata), Staghorn Sumac (Rhus typhina), Black Cherry (Prunus serotina) and Black Walnut (Juglans nigra) .
4. This tree can be identified by is palmately lobed leaves that turn brown in the fall. It also has green rounded nut that turns brown in the fall and splits apart exposing an edible hickory nut. It also has a distinctive shaggy bark where is gets the name Shagbark Hickory. 
5. The Shagbark Hickory can be found in moist soils, especially valleys and upland slopes in mixed hardwood forests. The name hickory comes from the American Indian word pawcohiccora, for oily food removed from pounded kernels steeped in boiling water. This hickory milk was used in cooking cakes and hominy. The inner bark can also be used to make a yellow dye.

description: In a large, mature, mostly publicly owned forest tract on a gradual north-facing slope, dominated by red oak and red maple, uncommon for Worcester County. Mature, tall white pine occurs  in small patches mostly on the east side, where 200 year old stone walls are prominent, some of which are double wide indicating formerly plowed fields and the presence of deeper, richer soil. An additional feature is the complete absence of woody invasive species. Mountain laurel and witch hazel are uncommon, in contrast to much of the surrounding area forests. White birch is more common than black birch, another unusual feature. White ash is occasional, some have been attacked by emerald ash borer and are dying out. Hemlock is occasional and no longer casting a deep shade, having been affected by hemlock wooly adelgid. Since I had a metric diameter tape handy, I decided to use it, both to give a more accurate sense of this stand, and to allow future biologists to directly compare.
